name: Djerma / Zarma
confidence_why: 6 independent first-hand descriptions agree (5 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Cooper, Paul V. & Oliver Rice. 1966. Djerma Basic Course. (Peace Corps / ERIC ED143238). Secondary: Wikipedia 'Zarma language' (raw wikitext downloaded 2026-09-12) reporting Hamani, Abdou (1980) La structure grammaticale du zarma; ELLAF 'Zarma' page (S. Bornand)…
catalog_locator: Cooper & Rice 1966, Introduction pp. x-xi (ERIC pp. 11-12), sections 'Stress' and 'Tone'; Wikipedia section 'Lexical tone and stress'; ELLAF language summa…
catalog_quote: Stress. Many Djerma utterances contain a succession of monosyllables more or less evenly stressed. In most two-syllable words, stress is on the first syllable. The last syllable of some two-syllable words, however, appears to receive as much stress as the first syllable, if not more. In three- and four-syllable words, primary stress is on the first syllable with a secondary stress on the third syllable. Tone. The function of tone in Djerma is a subject in need of more study. Djerma words exist having two or more different meanings, which appear to be distinguished, in isolation, only by a difference in tone. However, when these same words are uttered within the context of a sentence, the tonal distinction is blurred, and it is often difficult to detect the difference in tone heard previously when the word was uttered in isolation. Tonal distinctions must be learned as they occur.
sweep_summary: One target item (Ducroz & Charles 1979, Glottolog ref 128378) was already held by the project from an earlier compilation (HAL hal-05457575, whole issue of Études linguistiques 1(1), Niamey) and was re-read in full: it is a 28-page tonal analysis of the Kaado dialect of the Gorouol (three distinctive tones H/L/falling with minimal pairs at p. 52, tone-scheme inventories pp. 52-55, sandhi rule and terracing pp. 76-77) and contains no mention of stress or accent at all; it confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding and is silent on stress placement (Glottolog's page range 50-75 should read 50-77). Two further open HAL PDFs were downloaded this search of works with stress in the title and saved with entries under Nicolaï 1978 'Esquisse phonologique du parler de la région de Dolbel' (Annales Univ. Niamey 1: 197-234), whose tone section pp. 231-233 posits a 4-tone system for the same Kaado dialect 'parallèle à celui du zarma et du dendi' with no accent; and Nicolaï 1978 'Sur le songhay oriental', which discusses accent only for Gao Songhay (a different language) and characterises Niger Songhay in passing as tonal with 2 or 4 tones. Nothing read contradicts the catalog; nothing read gives a stress-position statement better than Cooper & Rice 1966, so the deciding source is not superseded, though Ducroz & Charles 1979 and Nicolaï 1978 (Dolbel) deserve to be added as first-hand tonal primaries. Still unread and highest-priority for a direct Zarma-proper statement on tone vs accent: Nicolaï 1976 (Bull. IFAN B 38(1): 67-126; HAL record hal-05503086 without file), plus the previously listed Tersis 1972, Hamani 1981 and the Hima 2001 Dosso-Zarma/Dolbel-Kaado tonology thesis (theses.fr 2001NICE2028, abstract only). HAL's web pages are behind an Anubis challenge for browser user-agents; the direct /file/ URLs served the PDFs to the default client.

new_statements.quote: « La hauteur mélodique des voyelles connaît plusieurs registres. Ceux retenus par le parler du Gorouol pour assumer une fonction distinctive sont au nombre de trois : haut (H), bas (B), descendant (D). [...] Bas / Haut : à dì "il a pris" – à dí "il a vu" ; à tà "il a accepté" – à tá "il a cousu" [...] Bas / Descendant : à dì "il a pris" – à dî "il a brûlé" » (p. 52). « Le ton montant peut donc être prévu et il n'a pas d'autonomie phonologique, il n'appartient donc pas au système de la langue, à la différence des tons haut, bas, descendant. » (p. 53)
new_statements.translation: "The melodic height of vowels has several registers. Those retained by the Gorouol dialect to carry a distinctive function are three in number: high (H), low (B), falling (D). [...] Low / High: à dì 'he took' – à dí 'he saw'; à tà 'he accepted' – à tá 'he sewed' [...] Low / Falling: à dì 'he took' – à dî 'he burned'" (p. 52). "The rising tone can therefore be predicted and has no phonological autonomy; it does not belong to the system of the language, unlike the high, low and falling tones." (p. 53)
new_statements.citation: Ducroz, J. M. & M. C. Charles. 1979. Recherche sur la prosodie soŋey (parler kaado du Gorouol, Niger). Études linguistiques (Niamey) 1(1): 50-77.
new_statements.locator: printed p. 52, II.A 'Détermination des tons'; p. 53; p. 77, conclusion 11
new_statements.reading: First-hand, professional tonal analysis of the Kaado (Gorouol/Dolbel) dialect of the zarm1239 languoid: three lexically distinctive tones established by minimal pairs, tone-scheme inventories by syllable count, a syntagmatic sandhi rule and terracing. No stress or accent is mentioned anywhere in the article, so it gives no stress-placement statement; it is a tone statement that confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding and says nothing for or against the Cooper & Rice 1966 first-syllable stress tendency. Nicolaï 1978 (Dolbel sketch, pp. 231-233, downloaded from HAL) independently gives a 4-tone system for the same dialect 'parallel to Zarma and Dendi', also without any accent.

tone_statements.translation: In the Zarma and Dendi dialects we recognise two types of tones: simple tones /´/, /`/ and complex tones /ˇ/, /ˆ/. Complex tones are far less numerous than simple tones; they do not occur in all syllabic contexts … 6.3. From 'pre-Songhay' to the four-tone systems (Dendi and Zarma). Given the preceding hypotheses, the schemas of the four-tone systems are identical to those of 'pre-Songhay'; the only difference is the phonematic support of the unit of placement, which passes from the syllable to the mora.

sources.citation: Nicolaï, Robert. 1978. Esquisse phonologique du parler de la région de Dolbel (Arrondissement de Téra). Annales de l'Université de Niamey 1: 197-234.
sources.quote: p. 231: « Le système dolbélien se différencie de la plupart des autres systèmes relevés en songhay. Nous avons la possibilité de quatre oppositions tonales dans le cadre de la syllabe [...] Les tons montants (CV̌), que l'on trouve en zarma et en dendi, existent ici mais sont, du moins dans de nombreux idiolectes, très difficiles à différencier des tons hauts » ; p. 232: « nous admettons à Dolbel un système à 4 tons, parallèle à celui du zarma et du dendi. »
sources.locator: section '3. Système tonétique', printed pp. 231-233 (pp. 36-38); conclusion p. 234
sources.note: Nothing about stress or accent (no 'accent'/'intensité' in the text). Same Kaado dialect (Dolbel/Fantio, Gorouol) as Ducroz & Charles; posits four syllable tones (H, L, rising, falling) parallel to Zarma and Dendi, noting the H vs rising contrast is weak in many idiolects but recoverable from syntagmatic behaviour. Confirms tonal.

sources.citation: Hima, Oumarou. 2001. Problèmes de prosodie en songhay : recherches comparatives entre deux parlers nigériens : le zarma de Dosso et le kaado de Dolbel. Thèse de doctorat, Université de Nice (dir. R. Nicolaï). [theses.fr record 2001NICE2028, abstract only; thesis not online]
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.quote: Abstract: 'Cette thèse décrit quelques aspects de la tonologie de deux parlers songhay du Niger : le zarma de Dosso et le kaado de Dolbel ... downdrift, downstep, tons flottants, propagation tonale ... ces deux parlers ont un système tonal très proche puisque seul un ton les sépare : le ton modulé BH est attesté uniquement en zarma.' (abstract only; body not reached)
sources.note: The only dedicated tonology of Zarma (downstep, floating tones, spreading; LH contour only in Zarma); would settle whether any word-level stress/accent exists alongside tone, which our record leaves to a 1966 Peace Corps course and a Wikipedia report of Hamani.

sources.note: Nothing. The article is a tonal analysis of the Kaado dialect of the Gorouol (Dolbel): three distinctive tones H/L/falling established by minimal pairs in a fixed frame, tone-scheme inventories for mono-, di- and trisyllables (nominals, verbals, verbo-nominals), then syntagmatic tone sandhi (a final H of the first term raises the L of the first mora of the second term) and terracing (downdrift). The words 'accent', 'intensité', 'stress', 'proéminence' do not occur anywhere in the article (a full-text search for stress/accent the scanned, pp. 27-40); the only 'accent d'intensité' in the scanne…
